prelimsCapsule.coreConceptSummary: Public healthcare in India has evolved through flagship missions like the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM, launched in 2005, later subsumed into the National Health Mission alongside NUHM in 2013). This framework integrates demand-side financing mechanisms like Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) and entitlement-based service guarantees like Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram (JSSK) to reduce Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) and Infant Mortality Rate (IMR).
highYieldFacts: Fact 1: NRHM was launched on 12th April 2005 by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) to provide accessible, affordable, and quality healthcare to the rural population, especially vulnerable groups.
Fact 2: Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), launched in April 2005, is a 100% centrally sponsored scheme under NHM integrating cash assistance with institutional delivery among poor pregnant women.

Fact 3: Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram (JSSK), launched in June 2011, entitles all pregnant women delivering in public health institutions to absolutely free and cashless services, including drugs, diagnostics, blood, and diet, alongside free care for sick newborns up to 1 year.

Fact 4: Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHA) serve as the vital community-level human interface under NRHM/NHM, acting as a bridge between the rural population and public health services on a performance-based incentive model.

Fact 5: According to the latest Sample Registration System (SRS) Special Bulletin, India's Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) has declined significantly to 97 per 100,000 live births (2018-20), moving closer to the SDG target of less than 70 by 2030.
trapsAndElimination: Trap 1: Confusing JSY with JSSK. JSY is primarily a conditional cash transfer scheme for institutional deliveries targeted at Low Performing States (LPS), whereas JSSK is an entitlement-based, cashless service delivery scheme for both mother and sick infant irrespective of income status in public facilities.
Trap 2: Assuming NRHM covers only rural areas. While NRHM focuses on rural areas, the broader National Health Mission (NHM) incorporates both NRHM and the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM).
keyArticlesOrStatutes: Article 21 (Right to Health as part of Right to Life)
Directive Principles of State Policy: Articles 39(e), 41, 42, and 47 (Duty of the State to raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living and to improve public health)

mainsFramework.inDepthTheoryHtml:
Evolution and Architecture of India's Public Health Architecture

India's public health paradigm underwent a structural transformation with the launch of the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) in 2005. Designed to address systemic deficits in rural healthcare delivery, NRHM institutionalized decentralized planning, flexible financing, and community-led monitoring through ASHAs and Rogi Kalyan Samitis (Patient Welfare Committees). Recognizing the urban health deficit driven by rapid urbanization and slum growth, the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM) was integrated with NRHM in 2013 to form the overarching National Health Mission (NHM).

Demand-Side Financing and Entitlement Paradigms

To overcome financial barriers to institutional care, the architecture relies heavily on demand-side instruments such as the Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), which incentivizes institutional deliveries through direct cash transfers, categorizing states into Low Performing States (LPS) and High Performing States (HPS). Complementing JSY, the Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram (JSSK) introduced in 2011 moved beyond cash transfers to guarantee zero-out-of-pocket expenditure entitlements. JSSK mandates free drugs, diagnostics, blood transfusion, transport, and diet for pregnant women during normal and caesarean deliveries, as well as free diagnostics and treatment for sick newborns up to one year of age.

Structural Challenges and Governance Bottlenecks

Despite notable gains in reducing Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) and Infant Mortality Rate (IMR), structural bottlenecks persist. India's total public health expenditure remains low (around 1.2-2.1% of GDP), well below the National Health Policy 2017 target of 2.5%. Severe infrastructure deficits, rural-urban disparities in specialist availability, and high out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE) driven by private sector reliance continue to plague the system. Furthermore, supply-chain inefficiencies in drug procurement and variable implementation capacities across states hinder optimal resource utilization.

dimensions.constitutional_or_legal: Grounded in Directive Principles of State Policy (Article 47) and judicial expansion of Article 21, interpreting health as an enforceable fundamental right.
dimensions.socio_economic: Reduces catastrophic health expenditures for marginalized households, breaks intergenerational poverty traps caused by medical debt, and empowers women through ASHAs and conditional cash transfers.
dimensions.administrative_governance: Requires rigorous cooperative federalism, decentralized district-level micro-planning, robust digital tracking via HMIS (Health Management Information System), and convergence with Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM).
dimensions.international_or_comparative: Aligns with United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being) and Universal Health Coverage (UHC) principles.

prelims.question: With reference to the Indian public health system, consider the following statements: 1. Under Janani Suraksha Yojana, institutional delivery is incentivized for all pregnant women irrespective of economic status. 2. Rural Health Mission provides for a Village Health and Sanitation Committee in every village. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
prelims.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect because JSY is primarily targeted at poor pregnant women (with special focus on Low Performing States, though BPL/SC/ST women in High Performing States also qualify), rather than 'all pregnant women irrespective of economic status'. Statement 2 is correct as NRHM mandates Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Committees (VHSNC) at the village level.

modelMainsQA.question: Examine the role of flagship public health interventions such as NRHM, JSY, and JSSK in transforming India's maternal and child health landscape. What are the persistent structural hurdles in achieving universal health coverage? (250 Words, 15 Marks)

approach.intro: Define the scope of public health interventions under the National Health Mission (NHM), linking it to constitutional mandates (Article 21 and 47) and SDG 3.
approach.body: Analyze the specific contributions of NRHM (infrastructure/ASHA), JSY (demand-side financing), and JSSK (cashless entitlements). Highlight remaining systemic hurdles: low public spending, human resource deficits, and out-of-pocket expenditure.
approach.conclusion: Suggest a forward-looking path emphasizing primary healthcare strengthening, digital health integration, and increased budgetary allocations.

modelMainsQA.modelAnswerHtml:
Public healthcare in India underwent a paradigm shift with the launch of the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) in 2005, later integrated into the National Health Mission (NHM). By blending infrastructure strengthening with demand-side incentives and entitlement guarantees, these interventions have structurally redefined maternal and child healthcare (MCH) in India.

Transformative Impact of NRHM, JSY, and JSSK

  • Decentralized Infrastructure and Community Interface (NRHM): NRHM revitalized Sub-Centres, Primary Health Centres (PHCs), and Community Health Centres (CHCs). The creation of the Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) cadre bridged the gap between marginalized communities and institutional care.
  • Demand-Side Financing (JSY): By integrating conditional cash transfers with institutional deliveries, JSY successfully incentivized poor and rural women to opt for institutional care, dramatically driving down home deliveries.
  • Entitlement-Based Zero-Expense Care (JSSK): Moving beyond cash transfers, JSSK guaranteed absolute cashless services—free drugs, diagnostics, blood, and transport—for pregnant women and sick newborns up to one year, mitigating catastrophic financial shocks.

Consequently, India's Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) has dropped significantly to 97 per 100,000 live births, bringing the nation closer to SDG 3 targets.

Persistent Structural Hurdles

  • Inadequate Public Expenditure: India's public health spending hovers around 1.2-2.1% of GDP, well short of the 2.5% recommended by the National Health Policy 2017, perpetuating heavy reliance on the private sector.
  • Human Resource Deficits: Severe shortages of specialists, obstetricians, and pediatricians in rural and semi-urban public health facilities create operational bottlenecks.
  • High Out-of-Pocket Expenditure (OOPE): Despite schemes like JSSK, procurement delays and out-of-stock medicines force patients to bear high out-of-pocket expenses for diagnostics and drugs.

Way Forward

To achieve true Universal Health Coverage (UHC), India must scale up public health investments to 2.5% of GDP, institutionalize robust supply-chain management through digital governance (Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission), and transform Sub-Centres into fully functional Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (Health and Wellness Centres) focusing on comprehensive primary care.

practiceMCQs.question: Which of the following components are explicitly covered under the Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram (JSSK)? 1. Free and cashless delivery in public health institutions. 2. Free transport from home to institution and drop-back. 3. Free treatment for sick newborns up to one year of age. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
practiceMCQs.explanation: JSSK entitles all pregnant women delivering in public health institutions to free drugs, diagnostics, blood, diet, and free transport from home to facility, between facilities in case of referral, and drop-back. It also covers free treatment and diagnostics for sick newborns up to one year of age.

practiceMCQs.question: Consider the following statements regarding the Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) under the National Health Mission: 1. ASHA is a government employee drawing a fixed monthly salary decided by the Central Government. 2. She acts as a key link between the health system and the rural community. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceMCQs.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect because ASHAs are voluntary community health workers who receive performance-based incentives for specific activities rather than a fixed government employee salary. Statement 2 is correct as they serve as the primary link between the community and public health infrastructure.
